title: Dense vector retrieval
summary: Dense retrieval embeds the query and every chunk into vectors and returns the nearest chunks. It matches meaning rather than words, and it always returns neighbours, relevant or not.
useIf: Users paraphrase, describe symptoms in their own words or search across languages, and the documents use different vocabulary.
avoidIf: Queries hinge on rare entities, codes or exact strings and you have no keyword leg beside the vectors.

explain.md: A **bi-encoder** embedding model maps text to a vector. Chunks are embedded once at ingestion. At query time the query goes through the same model and an approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) index returns the closest chunks by cosine similarity or another metric. Because query and chunk never see each other inside the model, millions of chunks can be searched fast [[tr7]].

explain.title: Dense retrieval at query time
explain.alt: A query is embedded, searched in a vector index, and the nearest chunks come back with similarity scores.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant E as Embedding model
  participant I as Vector index
  U->>E: Query text
  E->>I: Query vector
  I-->>U: Top k chunks and scores

explain.md: **Strengths.** Synonyms, paraphrase and conceptual questions match without shared words. Azure puts it this way: the advantage of vector search is finding information that is conceptually similar to the query even when no keyword matches [[r43]].

**Weaknesses.** In the EntityQuestions study, dense retrievers drastically underperformed sparse methods on simple entity-rich questions, and generalised only to common entities unless the question pattern was seen in training [[tr2]]. BEIR found dense models often weaker than BM25 out of domain [[r11]]. Two operational traps follow. First, **nearest neighbours always exist**, so a gibberish query still returns k chunks. You need a threshold or an abstention rule. Azure's vector `threshold` (preview in `2026-08-01-preview`) drops weak matches before fusion even when fewer than `k` remain [[r35]]. Second, scores are model specific: Azure documents cosine similarity from 0.333 to 1.00, and a cutoff tuned for one embedding model is wrong for another [[r1]].

explain.title: Clean the query like the chunks
explain.md: Apply the same text normalisation to the query that you applied to chunks before embedding, for example lowercasing. A mismatch quietly lowers similarity [[r8]].

whereToUse: Help-centre and FAQ search where users describe problems in their own words
Cross-language retrieval with a multilingual embedding model
The vector leg of hybrid search, paired with BM25
Recommendation of related documents or similar tickets

use: Paraphrase and vocabulary mismatch are common
You can test several embedding models on your own queries
Documents are prose rather than codes or tables
You have a plan for thresholds and abstention
avoid: Queries are mostly identifiers, names or exact phrases
The domain is highly specialised and the embedding model has not seen it
You cannot afford re-embedding when you change models
flips: Exact-match failures appear in the logs: add a BM25 leg and fuse
Domain jargon is rare: evaluate a domain-tuned or larger model on labelled queries
Weak matches reach the model: add a vector threshold or a reranker-based cutoff

pitfalls.symptom: A query for a part number returns thematically related parts
pitfalls.cause: The embedding blurs rare tokens into a neighbourhood of similar text
pitfalls.fix: Add a keyword leg and fuse, or route identifier-shaped queries to BM25

pitfalls.symptom: Nonsense questions still produce confident answers
pitfalls.cause: Nearest-neighbour search returns k results regardless of relevance
pitfalls.fix: Apply a vector threshold or a reranker cutoff and let the system abstain

pitfalls.symptom: Scores shift after an embedding model upgrade and cutoffs break
pitfalls.cause: Similarity distributions are specific to the model
pitfalls.fix: Recalibrate thresholds on a labelled set whenever the model or version changes

scenarios.title: FAQ bot over two thousand questions
scenarios.situation: A consumer product has a stable FAQ of about two thousand entries. Customers phrase questions in many ways, and the FAQ never contains codes.
unknowns: Are there product names or SKUs in queries?
scenarios.question: Which retrieval design fits?

options.name: Dense retrieval with a similarity threshold and a fallback message
options.why: Paraphrase is where dense retrieval shines, the corpus is small and a threshold handles no-answer queries.
options.tradeoff: Threshold needs calibration on real queries and recalibration if the model changes.

options.name: Hybrid with semantic ranker
options.why: Handles any identifiers that appear later.
options.tradeoff: More cost and moving parts than this corpus needs today.

options.name: BM25 only
options.why: Customer wording rarely matches FAQ wording.
options.tradeoff: Right when users search with exact product names or error codes.

flips.if: Customers start pasting order numbers or SKUs
flips.then: Add a BM25 leg and fuse.

flips.if: The FAQ grows to millions of entries and memory cost becomes the main concern
flips.then: Keep dense retrieval but compress vectors with quantization and test recall, instead of adding a second engine.

scenarios.takeaway: Paraphrase traffic is the dense sweet spot.

scenarios.title: Patent-style corpus with rare terms
scenarios.situation: Analysts search a large corpus of technical filings. Queries contain rare compound names and numbered claims alongside conceptual descriptions.
unknowns: Is the embedding model trained on this domain?
scenarios.question: Can you ship dense retrieval alone?

options.name: Hybrid retrieval and measure recall@k against dense-only on the labelled queries
options.why: Rare entities are the known weak spot of dense retrievers [[tr2]], and the labelled set tells you how much the keyword leg adds.
options.tradeoff: Two retrievals per query and a fusion step to tune.

options.name: Dense only with a larger embedding model
options.why: A bigger model can still fail on rare strings, and you pay more for every re-embedding.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable if the evaluation shows no gain from a keyword leg.

options.name: BM25 only
options.why: Strong on the rare terms and out of domain.
options.tradeoff: Misses conceptual descriptions with different vocabulary.

flips.if: Evaluation shows dense-only matches hybrid recall
flips.then: Drop the keyword leg and save a retrieval.

flips.if: Recall on rare compound names is the weak slice
flips.then: Keep the keyword leg and weight it up for those queries; a larger embedding model rarely fixes exact-token misses.

scenarios.takeaway: Measure the keyword leg's lift before you drop it.

quiz.q: A vector-only assistant answers a nonsense question with a confident answer from an unrelated chunk. What is the most direct cause?
options: The embedding model is too small
Nearest-neighbour search always returns k results and nothing stops weak ones
quiz.explain: Dense search returns the nearest vectors whatever their distance. A threshold or abstention rule is what filters them. Index corruption and model size are not required to produce this behaviour, and BM25 is not part of a vector-only design.

quiz.q: Which change in traffic most clearly argues for adding a keyword leg to a dense retriever?
options: More queries containing part numbers and error codes
quiz.explain: Exact tokens are the dense blind spot [[tr2]]. Longer questions and more users do not change retrieval mode, and chunk size is a separate dial.

quiz.q: Select the true statements about thresholds on vector similarity.
options: They are specific to the embedding model
They can drop weak matches before fusion
A threshold tuned on one model carries over to another unchanged
They remove the need for evaluation
quiz.explain: Similarity distributions depend on the model, and Azure's preview vector threshold drops weak matches before fusion [[r35]]. A threshold does not transfer across models and still needs a labelled set to tune.

flashcards.front: Why does dense retrieval return results for a nonsense query?
flashcards.back: Nearest-neighbour search always returns the k closest vectors. Only a threshold or abstention rule can stop weak ones.

flashcards.front: What did EntityQuestions show about dense retrievers?
flashcards.back: They drastically underperformed sparse methods on simple entity-rich questions, generalising only to common entities.

flashcards.front: Why must the query be cleaned like the chunks?
flashcards.back: A normalisation mismatch between query and chunk text, such as casing, quietly lowers similarity.
